# Inguinal hernia

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Hernias > Inguinal hernia*

[Original Article Link](/library/zh0rgf)

---

## Summary

An inguinal <u>hernia</u> is an abnormal protrusion of intra-abdominal contents (most commonly fat) through the <u>inguinal canal</u>. Inguinal <u>hernias</u> are the most common type of groin <u>hernia</u>, and can be further subdivided based on anatomic location: an <u>indirect inguinal hernia</u> protrudes <u>lateral</u> to the inferior epigastric vessels through the <u>deep inguinal ring</u>, whereas a <u>direct inguinal hernia</u> protrudes <u>medial</u> to the inferior epigastric vessels through a defect in the <u>posterior</u> wall of the <u>inguinal canal</u>. An <u>uncomplicated inguinal hernia</u> typically manifests as a mass in the groin with or without <u>pain</u> (<u>inguinodynia</u>). Incarceration, obstruction, and strangulation of hernial contents are collectively referred to as <u>complicated inguinal hernia</u>. Inguinal <u>hernia</u> is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>. Imaging, preferably with <u>ultrasound</u>, is indicated if the <u>clinical diagnosis</u> is uncertain. <u>Surgery</u> is the only definitive <u>management of inguinal hernia</u> and can be performed as an open <u>surgery</u> or laparoscopically. A <u>strangulated inguinal hernia</u> is a surgical emergency. In patients with an <u>incarcerated hernia</u> with or without <u>bowel obstruction</u>, manual reduction of the <u>hernia</u> may be considered as a temporizing measure before <u>surgery</u>. <u>Conservative management</u> may be considered in selected adult patients with a small, <u>uncomplicated inguinal hernia</u>; timely surgical intervention is recommended in children due to the risk for <u>complicated inguinal hernia</u>.

---

## Definitions

* <u>Direct inguinal hernia</u>: protrusion of abdominal and/or <u>pelvic</u> contents directly through the <u>posterior</u> wall of the <u>inguinal canal</u>

* <u>Indirect inguinal hernia</u>: protrusion of abdominal and/or <u>pelvic</u> contents into the <u>inguinal canal</u> through the <u>deep inguinal ring</u>

* Scrotal hernia: a large, <u>indirect inguinal hernia</u> that descends through the <u>inguinal canal</u> into the <u>scrotum</u>

* <u>Uncomplicated inguinal hernia</u>: an inguinal <u>hernia</u> that is completely reducible and not associated with <u>signs of bowel obstruction</u> or strangulation

* <u>Complicated inguinal hernia</u>: an inguinal <u>hernia</u> that is either irreducible (incarcerated) or associated with <u>mechanical bowel obstruction</u> and/or strangulation

* Occult inguinal hernia: an inguinal <u>hernia</u> that is not identifiable on <u>physical examination</u>

## Epidemiology

* <u>Prevalence</u>

* 5–10% In the US [[2]](/library/F30g4f)

* Inguinal <u>hernias</u> are the most common <u>type of hernias</u> (∼ 75% of all cases). [[3]](/library/t30X4f)

* <u>Indirect inguinal hernia</u> > <u>direct inguinal hernia</u>

* Responsible for one of the most common general surgical procedures in the United States  [[2]](/library/F30g4f)

* Sex: <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u>

* Age

* <u>Indirect inguinal hernia</u>: most commonly seen in male <u>infants</u> and older men

* <u>Direct inguinal hernia</u>: most commonly seen in older men




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Anatomy

### Inguinal canal




* Extends between the deep (internal) and <u>superficial</u> (external) ring

* Roof (superior): <u>internal oblique</u> and <u>transversus abdominis</u> muscles

* Floor (inferior): <u>inguinal ligament</u> (shelving edge of <u>external oblique</u>) and <u>lacunar ligament</u> (medially)

* <u>Posterior</u> wall: <u>transversalis fascia</u> laterally; <u>conjoint tendon</u> medially

* <u>Anterior</u> wall: <u>external oblique</u> <u>aponeurosis</u> and <u>internal oblique muscle</u> laterally





![Inguinal canal and spermatic cord](media/isjynul1cs2d5whluzzu5hib.jpg)

Inguinal canal and spermatic cord




### Hesselbach triangle borders




* Medially: <u>rectus abdominis muscle</u>

* Laterally: inferior epigastric vessels

* Inferiorly: <u>inguinal ligament</u>





![Borders of the inguinal canal and contents of the spermatic cord](media/oim8ktyogcdx3t261uvfvg9r.jpg)

## Pathophysiology

### Direct inguinal hernia




* Acquired condition

* Caused by weakening of the <u>transversalis fascia</u>

* Commonly secondary to conditions resulting in increased <u>intraabdominal pressure</u>  (e.g., <u>chronic obstructive pulmonary disease</u> with chronic <u>coughing</u>, <u>constipation</u>)

* May be associated with long-term <u>glucocorticoid</u> use

* <u>Medial</u> to the inferior epigastric <u>blood vessels</u> (within <u>Hesselbach triangle</u>) and <u>lateral</u> to the <u>rectus abdominis</u>

* Hernial sac protrudes directly through the <u>posterior</u> wall of the <u>inguinal canal</u> (without involvement of the <u>spermatic cord</u> or <u>round ligament of the uterus</u>)

* Only herniates through the <u>superficial</u> (external) ring

* Only surrounded by the <u>external spermatic fascia</u>





### Indirect inguinal hernia




* Most commonly results from incomplete obliteration of <u>processus vaginalis</u>;   during <u>fetal development</u> (but can also be acquired)

* May not become apparent until adulthood despite being present since <u>birth</u>.

* <u>Lateral</u> to the inferior epigastric <u>blood vessels</u> (outside <u>Hesselbach triangle</u>)

* Runs from the deep inguinal ring through the <u>inguinal canal</u> to the <u>superficial (external) inguinal ring</u> (in men, along with the <u>spermatic cord</u>)

* Surrounded by the <u>external spermatic fascia</u>, cremasteric muscle fibers, and <u>internal spermatic fascia</u>

* <u>Indirect inguinal hernia</u> may be associated with a <u>communicating hydrocele</u>.





> [!NOTE]
> "The DIRECT path leads through the MiDdle, the INDIRECT path goes beLow." (DIRECT <u>hernias</u> lie MeDial and INDIRECT <u>hernias</u> lie Lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels)




References:[[2]](/library/F30g4f)[[3]](/library/t30X4f)[[4]](/library/930Nkf)[[5]](/library/x30Ekf)

## Clinical features

### Uncomplicated inguinal hernia [[6]](/library/4nb3t8)[[7]](/library/znbrD8)[[8]](/library/uz0pui)




* Typically manifests as an ill-defined mass in the inguinal region with the following features: 

* Increases in size when <u>coughing</u> or straining

* Decreases in size on lying <u>supine</u>

* Inguinal <u>pain</u>;  (<u>inguinodynia</u>) or vague inguinal discomfort that increases with physical activity; can also be painless

* <u>Inguinodynia</u> with no palpable groin mass is typically the only manifestation of an <u>occult inguinal hernia</u>. [[9]](/library/OnbIt8)

* <u>Physical examination</u> 

* Ask the patient to perform the <u>Valsalva maneuver</u> and observe for an expansile <u>cough</u> impulse in the inguinal region.

* Palpate the inguinal canal. 

* Male patients: Invaginate the scrotal <u>skin</u> toward the <u>superficial inguinal ring</u> with the index or little finger.

* Female patients: Palpate the area over the <u>inguinal ligament</u>.

* Ask the patient to perform the <u>Valsalva maneuver</u>.

* A palpable bulge confirms the diagnosis of an inguinal <u>hernia</u>.

* The <u>hernia</u> is completely reducible and soft.





> [!TIP]
> Female patients rarely present with visible bulges but often report a sensation of heaviness or dull discomfort in the groin or <u>pelvis</u> that is worsened by lifting, straining, or prolonged standing. [[10]](/library/Hd1Krf0)




![Palpation of the inguinal canal in a male patient](media/okp32bp7slcto5h8noh8bjnm.jpg)

Palpation of the inguinal canal in a male patient

![Inguinal hernia](media/ifvq3dkqjbcxh29b0mz3x6gs.jpg)

Inguinal hernia




### Complicated inguinal hernia [[7]](/library/znbrD8)[[8]](/library/uz0pui)[[11]](/library/onb088)




* Incarcerated hernia

* The <u>hernia</u> is irreducible.

* <u>Skin</u> overlying the <u>hernia</u>: normal

* Obstructed hernia: : symptoms of <u>mechanical bowel obstruction</u> (sudden onset of <u>pain</u>, <u>nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>, abdominal distention, <u>constipation</u> or <u>obstipation</u>)

* Strangulated hernia

* Sudden, severe groin <u>pain</u> caused by constriction and <u>ischemia</u> (or <u>necrosis</u>) of hernial contents

* <u>Signs of sepsis</u> or <u>signs of shock</u>

* Features of <u>bowel obstruction</u> if the <u>hernia</u> contains intestinal loops

* <u>Skin</u> overlying the <u>hernia</u>: warm, <u>erythematous</u>, tender, and may appear exfoliated or blistered





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Manual reduction of an inguinal hernia</u> should not be attempted if there are any signs of <u>strangulated hernia</u>!




![Reducible, irreducible, and strangulated hernias](media/nhujj3rnewazuhm3tuu81pgo.jpg)

Reducible, irreducible, and strangulated hernias

## Diagnosis

Inguinal <u>hernia</u> is typically a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>; however, imaging may be useful if the <u>clinical diagnosis</u> is unclear or to investigate an underlying cause.




### Clinical evaluation




* <u>Medical history</u> should include:

* Identification of typical clinical features (e.g., of <u>uncomplicated inguinal hernia</u>)

* Onset and duration of symptoms  [[12]](/library/yd1dsf0)

* Evaluation of <u>risk factors</u> for an acquired inguinal <u>hernia</u>.

* <u>Physical examination</u> should include:

* <u>Palpation of the inguinal canal</u>

* Evaluation for signs of <u>complicated inguinal hernia</u>

* Identification of signs of underlying etiologies, e.g., <u>ascites</u>, <u>BPH</u>





> [!WARNING]
> To avoid missing inguinal <u>hernias</u>, routinely <u>examine the inguinal canal</u> in patients with unexplained <u>acute abdominal pain</u> and/or <u>clinical features of bowel obstruction</u>, especially in those with verbal impairment.




### Imaging for inguinal hernia [[6]](/library/4nb3t8)[[13]](/library/knbmt8)




#### Indications




* Uncertain <u>clinical diagnosis</u>

* Suspected recurrent or <u>occult inguinal hernia</u>

* Consider preoperative imaging for <u>complicated inguinal hernia</u>.





#### Modalities [[6]](/library/4nb3t8)




* First line: <u>ultrasound</u> of the groin  [[7]](/library/znbrD8)[[13]](/library/knbmt8)

* Inconclusive <u>ultrasound</u> findings: CT or <u>MRI</u> abdomen and <u>pelvis</u>

* <u>Complicated inguinal hernia</u>: Consider CT abdomen and <u>pelvis</u> with IV contrast.  [[11]](/library/onb088)[[14]](/library/SRXymB)

* Suspected <u>occult inguinal hernia</u> or recurrent inguinal <u>hernia</u>; consider any of the following modalities: [[9]](/library/OnbIt8)

* <u>MRI</u> groin [[15]](/library/hRXc5B)

* Dynamic CT or dynamic <u>MRI</u>, if available

* <u>Herniography</u>  [[15]](/library/hRXc5B)[[16]](/library/nnb7F8)[[17]](/library/lRXvMB)





#### Supportive findings




* Visualization of the hernial sac with its contents (e.g., bowel, <u>omentum</u>)

* <u>Uncomplicated inguinal hernia</u>

* Visible <u>expansile cough impulse</u>

* <u>Direct inguinal hernia</u>: fascial defect in the <u>posterior</u> wall of the <u>inguinal canal</u>

* <u>Indirect inguinal hernia</u>: widening of the <u>deep inguinal ring</u>

* <u>Obstructed hernia</u> [[18]](/library/IJbYvu)

* Free fluid and thickening of bowel wall within the hernial sac

* Dilated bowel loops within the abdomen (see “<u>Radiological signs of mechanical bowel obstruction</u>” for details)

* <u>Strangulated inguinal hernia</u> [[19]](/library/KnbU88)[[20]](/library/Xxb9ED)

* Absence of blood flow to the hernial contents

* Absence of <u>peristalsis</u> in bowel loops within the hernial sac





> [!WARNING]
> Do not delay emergency <u>surgery</u> for imaging in unstable patients with signs of <u>strangulated hernia</u> or <u>obstructed hernia</u>. [[6]](/library/4nb3t8)




### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[19]](/library/KnbU88)




The following tests should be obtained in patients with <u>strangulated inguinal hernia</u> or <u>incarcerated inguinal hernia</u> with <u>bowel obstruction</u> for supportive diagnostic evidence and to assess for complications. [[21]](/library/06beju)




* <u>CBC</u>

* Blood <u>glucose</u>

* Serum <u>electrolytes</u>

* <u>BMP</u>

* Serum <u>lactate</u>

* <u>Urinalysis</u>





> [!TIP]
> Maintain a high index of suspicion for strangulation in patients with an <u>incarcerated hernia</u> and <u>leukocytosis</u>. [[12]](/library/yd1dsf0)

| Femoral <u>lymphadenopathy</u> |  | <br><br>* <u>Sexually transmitted infection</u> (e.g., <u>chancroid</u>, <u>lymphogranuloma venereum</u>)<br><br>* Lower-extremity infection<br><br>* <u>Malignancy</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Lymph node</u> enlargement below the <u>inguinal ligament</u>, <u>medial</u> to the <u>femoral artery</u><br><br>* Benign: tender, soft, mobile<br><br>* Malignant: nontender, hard, fixed<br><br>* <u>Skin</u> changes, local <u>erythema</u><br><br>* <u>B symptoms</u><br><br>* Pulsatile when located over the <u>femoral artery</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Clinical<br><br>* <u>Ultrasound</u> to evaluate <u>lymph nodes</u><br><br>* Further diagnostics are required if <u>malignancy</u> is suspected<br><br><br> | <br>* Treatment of underlying cause<br><br> |
| Femoral arteriovenous fistula |  | <br><br>* <u>Iatrogenic</u> (most common): access for percutaneous cardiovascular procedures<br><br>* Trauma: penetrating injury to the lower extremity<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Initially asymptomatic<br><br>* Vibratory sensation, <u>bruit</u>, or pulses in the groin<br><br>* Lower extremity <u>ischemia</u><br><br>* Chronic <u>fistulas</u><br><br>* Limb <u>edema</u><br><br>* <u>High-output heart failure</u><br><br>* Arterial degeneration<br><br>* Fatigue<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Doppler ultrasound</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Small: observation<br><br>* Symptomatic, large, or do not seal spontaneously: surgical repair<br><br><br> |
| <u>Psoas abscess</u> |  | <br><br>* Infection<br><br>* Injury<br><br>* <u>Iatrogenic</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Fever</u><br><br>* Lower back or flank <u>pain</u><br><br>* Painful or painless mass<br><br>* <u>Psoas sign</u><br><br>* <u>Anorexia</u>, weight loss<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Clinical<br><br>* <u>Confirmatory test</u>: <u>CT scan</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Drainage<br><br>* <u>Antibiotics</u><br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Femoral artery aneurysm</u><br> |  | <br><br>* Arterial wall weakening<br><br>* <u>Atherosclerosis</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* May be asymptomatic<br><br>* Painless, pulsatile inguinal mass<br><br>* Signs and symptoms of <u>acute limb ischemia</u><br><br>* <u>Deep vein thrombosis</u><br><br>* Sudden leg <u>pain</u>, <u>weakness</u>, or numbness if <u>aneurysm</u> compresses nerves<br><br>* Continuous loud <u>murmur</u> on <u>auscultation</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Doppler ultrasound</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Small: observation<br><br>* Large and symptomatic: surgical repair<br><br><br> |





* <u>Hydrocele</u>

* <u>Varicocele</u>

* <u>Spermatocele</u>

* <u>Round ligament varicosities</u>

* Large cutaneous or subcutaneous masses in the inguinal region

* <u>Lipoma</u>

* <u>Sebaceous cyst</u>

* <u>Hematoma</u>

* See also “<u>Overview of scrotal abnormalities</u>.”





> [!TIP]
> A groin bulge with an <u>expansile cough impulse</u> above the <u>inguinal ligament</u> is diagnostic of an inguinal <u>hernia</u>. A <u>femoral hernia</u> typically manifests as a groin bulge below the <u>inguinal ligament</u> and <u>lateral</u> to the <u>pubic tubercle</u>. [[8]](/library/uz0pui)




### Groin <u>pain</u> [[7]](/library/znbrD8)




If these diagnoses are chronic or recurrent, they may cause <u>inguinodynia</u>.




* Sports hernia: chronic groin <u>pain</u> due to an injury or <u>weakness</u> of the <u>posterior</u> wall of the <u>inguinal canal</u>; an actual <u>hernia</u> may or may not be present [[22]](/library/Ad1Rsf0)

* <u>Muscular strain</u> or injury

* Pathology of the <u>hip joint</u>

* Lumbar <u>disk herniation</u>

* <u>Osteitis pubis</u>

* Neuropathy

* See also: “<u>Causes of pelvic pain</u>”





The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

## Management

### Overview  [[6]](/library/4nb3t8)[[7]](/library/znbrD8)




Critically ill patients with <u>complicated inguinal hernias</u> need to be stabilized and evaluated concurrently. Well-appearing patients with easily <u>reducible hernias</u> typically do not need further workup in the emergency department.




* <u>Complicated inguinal hernias</u>

* <u>Strangulated hernia</u> and/or signs of <u>mechanical bowel obstruction</u>: emergency <u>surgery</u> (within hours)

* <u>Incarcerated hernia</u> without strangulation: Consider <u>manual reduction of the inguinal hernia</u>. 

* Successful manual reduction: Close monitoring is required; consider <u>surgery</u> during the same hospital admission.

* Unsuccessful manual reduction: urgent <u>surgery</u>

* <u>Uncomplicated inguinal hernia</u>: Recommend elective <u>surgery</u>; consider <u>watchful waiting</u> in selected patients.





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Strangulated inguinal hernias</u> and <u>obstructed hernias</u> are surgical emergencies.




### Initial management and disposition [[19]](/library/KnbU88)[[23]](/library/a6bQju)




* All patients

* Assess <u>hernia</u> reducibility.

* Consider <u>ultrasound</u> if the diagnosis is unclear.

* Provide <u>analgesia</u> as needed.

* <u>Reducible hernia</u>: Refer for outpatient surgical management (<u>watchful waiting</u> or elective <u>hernia</u> repair).

* <u>Incarcerated hernia</u> 

* Provide resuscitation as needed; see “<u>ABCDE survey</u>.”

* Assess for signs of obstruction and strangulation.

* Establish <u>NPO</u> status  and provide <u>supportive care</u> as needed (e.g., <u>antiemetics</u>, <u>parenteral analgesics</u>, <u>fluid resuscitation</u>, and <u>electrolyte repletion</u>).

* No signs of <u>strangulated hernia</u>: Consider <u>manual reduction of the inguinal hernia</u> as a temporizing measure. [[23]](/library/a6bQju)[[24]](/library/h01cf20)

* Attempt to reduce the <u>hernia</u> 1–2 times.

* Consider admission or discharge after observation in the emergency department if reduction is successful.

* Consult <u>surgery</u> urgently for operative management if reduction is unsuccessful.

* Signs of <u>strangulated hernia</u>

* Consider <u>broad-spectrum IV antibiotics</u> (see “<u>Empiric antibiotic therapy for intraabdominal infection</u>”). [[25]](/library/1iX2qB)[[26]](/library/mpcVJW0)

* Consider <u>NG tube insertion</u> for <u>obstructed hernias</u>.

* Consult <u>surgery</u> urgently for operative management; do not attempt manual reduction.





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Intestinal infarction</u> can occur within 6 hours of strangulation. [[12]](/library/yd1dsf0)




> [!TIP]
> <u>Risk factors</u> associated with poor outcomes in incarcerated and <u>strangulated hernias</u> include older age, <u>obesity</u> (<u>BMI</u> > 30 kg/m<sup>2</sup>), prolonged duration of symptoms, female sex, and a delayed diagnosis. [[6]](/library/4nb3t8)

---

## Surgeries for inguinal hernia

* Surgical repair of the hernial defect is the only definitive treatment for inguinal <u>hernia</u>.

* The management of <u>direct inguinal hernia</u> and <u>indirect inguinal hernia</u> does not differ.

* Once the hernial contents are reduced (i.e., returned to the <u>abdominal cavity</u>), the goal of <u>hernia</u> <u>surgery</u> is to reinforce the <u>posterior</u> wall of the <u>inguinal canal</u> with a synthetic mesh or through primary tissue approximation.

* Emergency <u>surgery</u> is associated with an increased risk of complications; elective <u>surgery</u> is preferred when it is an option.





### Indications




* Elective <u>surgery</u>

* Significant <u>inguinodynia</u> limiting daily activities.

* Female patients

* Worsening of symptoms during <u>watchful waiting</u>.

* Patient prefers <u>surgery</u> to <u>watchful waiting</u>.

* Emergency <u>surgery</u>: <u>complicated inguinal hernia</u>





### Hernioplasty (mesh repair)




* Definition: repair of a hernial defect using a synthetic mesh

* Indication: <u>gold standard</u> for inguinal <u>hernia</u> repair [[6]](/library/4nb3t8)

* Open <u>surgery</u>

* Preferred in patients with <u>complicated inguinal hernia</u> or contraindications for <u>laparoscopic</u> repair  [[8]](/library/uz0pui)

* Procedures include Lichtenstein repair, in which a synthetic mesh is placed between the <u>transversalis fascia</u> and the <u>external oblique</u> <u>aponeurosis</u> to reinforce the <u>posterior</u> wall of the <u>inguinal canal</u>.   [[11]](/library/onb088)

* <u>Laparoscopic surgery</u>: preferred in patients with bilateral or recurrent inguinal <u>hernia</u> [[8]](/library/uz0pui)

* Transabdominal preperitoneal repair (TAPP): <u>laparoscopic</u>, preperitoneal mesh implementation between the <u>parietal peritoneum</u> and <u>transverse fascia</u>

* Total extraperitoneal repair (TEP): <u>laparoscopic</u>, extraperitoneal mesh implementation between <u>parietal peritoneum</u> and <u>transverse fascia</u>





![Lichtenstein repair](media/xatl59pkuv9ixakwa0h0ry0x.jpg)

Lichtenstein repair

![Transabdominal preperitoneal repair (TAPP)](media/th1pln63h5a9aed4gqe84nxg.jpg)

Transabdominal preperitoneal repair (TAPP)

![Total extraperitoneal repair (TEP)](media/tkds7c9fm29o31vhy6rpf409.jpg)

Total extraperitoneal repair (TEP)

![Mesh implementation during an endoscopic repair of an inguinal hernia](media/a4zrywysnzd0jkww6pfhqxvn.jpg)

Mesh implementation during an endoscopic repair of an inguinal hernia




### Herniorrhaphy (non-mesh repair)




* Definition: open surgical repair of a hernial defect using <u>autologous</u> tissue

* Indication: Consider in patients at high risk of <u>surgical site infection</u>.  [[8]](/library/uz0pui)[[25]](/library/1iX2qB)

* Options: Shouldice repair

* A pure tissue repair that involves a multilayer imbricated repair of the <u>posterior</u> wall of the <u>inguinal canal</u> with a <u>continuous running suture</u> technique.  [[8]](/library/uz0pui)

* Preferred procedure when <u>hernioplasty</u> is not feasible

* Has a lower recurrence rate than other non-mesh repairs

* Important consideration: <u>Herniorrhaphy</u> is associated with a greater risk of recurrence than <u>hernioplasty</u>. [[29]](/library/diXoqB)





![Shouldice repair](media/rrjwa314h9tdgh2zmlqc1sv9.jpg)

Shouldice repair

## Inguinal hernia in children

### <u>Epidemiology</u>




* <u>Incidence</u>: up to 5% in term <u>infants</u> and up to 20% in <u>preterm infants</u> [[32]](/library/NSV--F0)[[33]](/library/nSV7Z80)[[34]](/library/uSVpY80)

* <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> (4–5:1) [[33]](/library/nSV7Z80)[[34]](/library/uSVpY80)





### Etiology [[32]](/library/NSV--F0)[[33]](/library/nSV7Z80)




* Anatomical causes

* Indirect (most common): due to a <u>patent processus vaginalis</u>

* Direct (rare in children): due to weakening of the <u>transversalis fascia</u>

* <u>Risk factors</u> 

* Male sex

* <u>Premature birth</u>

* <u>Low birth weight</u>

* Increased <u>intra-abdominal pressure</u> (e.g., from <u>ventriculoperitoneal shunt</u>, <u>ascites</u>)

* <u>Family history</u>

* <u>Connective tissue disease</u>





### Clinical features [[33]](/library/nSV7Z80)




* Groin mass 

* More common on the right side (in ∼ 60% of patients)  [[32]](/library/NSV--F0)

* Increases in size with <u>coughing</u> or crying

* Can extend to the <u>scrotum</u> or <u>labia majora</u>

* May be reducible  or incarcerated [[32]](/library/NSV--F0)[[34]](/library/uSVpY80)

* Typically painless; large <u>hernias</u> can cause discomfort [[32]](/library/NSV--F0)[[34]](/library/uSVpY80)

* Features of associated conditions may be present, e.g.:

* Nonpalpable <u>testes</u> in <u>cryptorchidism</u> [[35]](/library/GcWBd40)

* Joint hypermobility, <u>skin hyperextensibility</u> in <u>connective tissue disorders</u> (e.g., <u>Ehlers-Danlos syndrome</u>) [[33]](/library/nSV7Z80)

* Ambiguous genitalia or palpable <u>testes</u> in <u>phenotypic</u> female individuals with <u>differences of sex development</u> (e.g., <u>androgen insensitivity syndrome</u>) [[34]](/library/uSVpY80)

* Features suggestive of incarcerated or <u>strangulated hernias</u> [[36]](/library/chVa180)

* Similar to those in adults; see "<u>Complicated inguinal hernia</u>."

* Inconsolable crying and fussiness suggests complicated <u>hernia</u> in nonverbal children.





> [!WARNING]
> In children, the risk of inguinal <u>hernia</u> incarceration is highest in <u>infancy</u>. [[32]](/library/NSV--F0)[[34]](/library/uSVpY80)




### Diagnosis [[33]](/library/nSV7Z80)[[34]](/library/uSVpY80)




* Inguinal <u>hernia</u> is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>. 

* A <u>reducible hernia</u> may be detectable only during crying or <u>coughing</u>.

* Use caregiver reports of intermittent mass in the groin as supportive evidence.

* <u>Laboratory studies</u> and imaging are not routinely indicated.

* <u>Ultrasound</u> may be used in case of diagnostic uncertainty. [[33]](/library/nSV7Z80)[[37]](/library/UhVbW80)





### Management [[32]](/library/NSV--F0)[[33]](/library/nSV7Z80)[[34]](/library/uSVpY80)




<u>Surgery</u> is recommended for all patients as <u>hernia</u> in children is associated with a significant risk of incarceration and, consequently, strangulation.




* <u>Reducible hernia</u> [[34]](/library/uSVpY80)

* Refer to a specialist (e.g., pediatric <u>surgery</u>, pediatric urology) for elective <u>surgery</u>.

* Timing of <u>surgery</u>  [[32]](/library/NSV--F0)[[33]](/library/nSV7Z80)

* Premature <u>neonates</u>: <u>Surgery</u> performed after discharge from <u>neonatal ICU</u> may be associated with optimal outcomes.  [[33]](/library/nSV7Z80)[[38]](/library/oSV0080)

* Older <u>infants</u> and children: Timing depends on patient factors such as risk of incarceration. [[32]](/library/NSV--F0)

* <u>Incarcerated hernia</u> [[33]](/library/nSV7Z80)[[34]](/library/uSVpY80)[[36]](/library/chVa180)

* Perform <u>manual reduction of the inguinal hernia</u>; sedation or <u>analgesia</u> may be required.

* Consult a specialist for urgent <u>surgery</u>.

* Timing of <u>surgery</u>

* <u>Irreducible hernia</u>: emergency <u>surgery</u> [[36]](/library/chVa180)

* Successful manual reduction: typically during the same admission (within 24 hours to 5 days) to minimize risk of recurrent incarceration  [[39]](/library/lQVvw80)[[40]](/library/ESV8Y80)

* <u>Strangulated hernia</u>

* Immediate referral for <u>surgery</u>.

* Initiate management for <u>pain</u> and associated complications (e.g., <u>bowel obstruction</u>, <u>shock</u>).

* Manual reduction is contraindicated.





#### <u>Hernia</u> <u>surgery</u> in children [[33]](/library/nSV7Z80)[[36]](/library/chVa180)




* <u>Herniorrhaphy</u> is typically performed; mesh repair (<u>hernioplasty</u>) may be considered in selected patients.

* <u>Surgery</u> can be performed using an open or <u>laparoscopic</u> approach.  [[32]](/library/NSV--F0)[[41]](/library/PhVWV80)

* Evaluation for <u>contralateral</u> <u>hernia</u> during <u>surgery</u> is controversial.  [[32]](/library/NSV--F0)[[33]](/library/nSV7Z80)[[34]](/library/uSVpY80)

* Counsel patients and/or caregivers on the small risk of recurrence.  [[32]](/library/NSV--F0)[[36]](/library/chVa180)
